title: Why I Use the Article of the Week in My Elective Classes
author: Bonnema, Heidi
summary: In this guest post, Heidi Bonnema, a newer teacher and colleague of Stuart's, explains why she uses Kelly Gallagher's Article of the Week in non-core electives such as Food and Nutrition and Career and Life Skills. Her claim is that the AoW can augment any content area: it replaces badly outdated textbook content with current, credible articles and engages students, some of whom start bringing articles to her. Its rubric splits points evenly between close reading and writing, which pushes students away from the habit of hunting for bolded answers and toward reading for meaning first. The They Say/I Say template gives students a repeatable structure for evidence, opinion and rebuttal, and her 250-word cap forces concision that employers value while keeping grading manageable. She concludes that AoWs combine transferable literacy habits with content relevant to her own subject, keeping students busy preparing for life rather than doing busy work.
points: Bonnema argues the Article of the Week can be added to any subject, including electives, because it augments rather than replaces the existing curriculum.
Current articles solve the problem of outdated textbooks, such as a 14-year-old nutrition text still touting Olestra, and tend to be more engaging for both students and teacher.
Weighting close reading at half the grade counters the familiar shortcut of skimming for bold words to answer chapter questions, and builds a lifelong habit of reading toward a purpose.
A strict 250-word limit with the They Say/I Say template trains succinct, evidence-backed writing and keeps grading load manageable.
quotes: The beauty of the article of the week is that it augments whatever curriculum you already have in place. I don’t know about you, but the textbooks our public school provides me with are pretty outdated. I think my current Food and Nutrition class textbook is 14 years old.

Now again, I don't know about you, but I don’t have time or energy to fight for new textbooks. I do, however, have access to credible online resources for information that I can pass on to my students that is far more up-to-date (thanks, Internet). Using the AoW rubric and standard format, it is easy to pop an AoW in my lesson plans to bring current information to whatever topic I’m teaching. Once I teach kids how to tackle an AoW a few times, they understand the process and consistently produce great results.

How often have we seen this scenario: A class is assigned “read chapter 4, answer questions 1-10.” The students open to the question page and begin to answer questions without reading the chapter at all. They hunt for the bold words, they find headings, and take shortcuts to get the assignment done and off their homework list.

The fact that close reading is half their grade is a super clear way to communicate the importance of the habit of reading toward a purpose — in the case of the AoW, it's reading toward the purpose of, first, understanding, and then second, entering the conversation of which the article is a part. If this becomes a habit, they will begin to close read in other subject areas, and their overall learning, retention, and application will produce students that are unstoppable.

I don’t let my kids go over 250 words (1 lined page in their written response). Again, I hate grading, and I don’t want to read crap (x75). I also don’t want to read 75 versions of the article rewritten with their opinions randomly inserted. They need to be direct, back up their thoughts with evidence, and give me quality, not quantity.

I believe kids need to be busy preparing for life — but not with mere busy work. That's why I use article of the week assignment in my elective classes: when my students apply themselves to the task, they develop solid literacy of all the good habits my students can get into if they use it well. All of the AoWs are current, relevant information, which has the potential to add depth to any subject. But probably most importantly, it combines the skills necessary for success in life and in other classes with content relevant to my class.
